account:
It is day 1, late morning. I inspected the mill stock for my ten o'clock appointment: eighty hay bales were available at two emeralds each. The neighbour says builder and freight want nineteen bales in exchange for thirty-two oak planks and agreed services, and that the innkeeper urgently needs grain and has mentioned credit or trade. Payment, rather than an absence of stock, appears to be the immediate difficulty, though I have not heard the proposed terms directly from these buyers or found the miller.

Several townsfolk have repeated an unusual report of a 'bridge or port change' at the bakery. One says baker and innkeeper were present, and another version includes freight. None has explained what actually changed. The neighbour has heard only the same vague rumour and cautioned against treating it as confirmed. I cannot yet tell whether this concerns a crossing, freight arrangements, or something else. Reports of baker and innkeeper carrying bread between the bakery, market streets and inn suggest bread distribution is active, but do not establish anything improper or connect it conclusively to the rumour. My tentative impression is that people are arranging grain, bread and perhaps transport or barter without my involvement; their exact purpose remains uncertain.

The town accounts are another unresolved matter. The secretary found no council records identifying who holds the missing account figures, and my treasury inspection found 128 emeralds but no account records. There is no evidence tying that issue to the grain negotiations or bakery rumour.

I should seek firsthand explanations rather than repeat speculation, while keeping today's remaining appointments: noon lunch at home, one o'clock council letters in the office, three o'clock tea at the neighbour's dockside cottage, half past four in the office, and six o'clock great hall lighting inspection with builder.
